findings.title: limitFunction drops all call arguments before invoking the wrapped function
findings.cause: The returned wrapper is `() => limit(() => function_())`, so it ignores every argument supplied by callers instead of forwarding `...arguments_` into the original function.
findings.impact: Any limited reusable function that depends on parameters receives `undefined` values. This breaks the documented reusable-function recipe (`limitedFetchUrl(url)`) and the exported TypeScript signature that promises argument-preserving wrappers.
findings.evidence: index.d.ts:133-136 declares `limitFunction<Arguments...>` returns `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`. recipes.md:161-163 calls `limitedFetchUrl(url)`. Runtime probe `limitFunction(async (value, suffix) => value + suffix, {concurrency:1})('a','b')` printed `NaN` because both arguments were lost.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited=limitFunction(async (value, suffix)=> value + suffix, {concurrency:1}); console.log(await limited('a','b'));"  # expected ab, actual NaN

findings.title: Options-object default enables rejectOnClear even though the documented default is false
findings.cause: When `concurrency` is an options object, destructuring uses `rejectOnClear = true` instead of the documented/default false value.
findings.impact: Calling `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` silently changes `clearQueue()` semantics: pending promises reject with `AbortError` even though the caller did not opt into rejection. Existing shutdown/queue-clearing flows can start rejecting `Promise.all` or unhandled pending promises unexpectedly.
findings.evidence: readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 say `rejectOnClear` is boolean with default `false`, and readme.md:104-105 says rejection occurs when enabled. Runtime probe with `pLimit({concurrency:1})` queued one pending task, called `clearQueue()`, and printed `rejected:AbortError`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const delay=ms=>new Promise(r=>setTimeout(r,ms)); const limit=pLimit({concurrency:1}); const running=limit(()=>delay(50)); const pending=limit(()=>delay(1)); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); console.log(await Promise.race([pending.then(()=>'fulfilled', e=>'rejected:'+e.name), delay(20).then(()=>'still-pending')])); await running;"  # expected still-pending, actual rejected:AbortError

findings.title: limit.map stops passing the index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: The mapper call conditionally passes `index` only when `Array.isArray(iterable)` is true; for Set, iterator, and other iterable inputs it passes `undefined` instead.
findings.impact: Code using documented `limit.map(iterable, mapperFunction)` semantics gets `undefined` indexes for supported iterable inputs. This breaks callers that key work, preserve offsets, or compute results from the mapper index.
findings.evidence: readme.md:78-85 says the mapper receives item value and index and is equivalent to `Array.from(iterable, (item, index) => limit(mapperFunction, item, index))`. index.d.ts:40-43 types the index as `number` for any `Iterable<Input>`. Runtime probe over `new Set(['a','b'])` returned `[ ['a', undefined], ['b', undefined] ]` (JSON prints undefined array slots as null).
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit=pLimit(2); console.log(JSON.stringify(await limit.map(new Set(['a','b']), (value,index)=> [value,index])));"  # expected [["a",0],["b",1]], actual [["a",null],["b",null]]

findings.title: rejectOnClear runtime validation accepts falsey non-boolean values
findings.cause: Validation is guarded by `rejectOnClear &&`, so non-boolean values such as `0`, empty string, and `null` skip the TypeError path whenever they are falsey.
findings.impact: JavaScript consumers can pass invalid option shapes that TypeScript and the docs reject, making configuration mistakes silently change behavior instead of failing fast.
findings.evidence: readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 specify `rejectOnClear` as boolean, and index.test-d.ts:28-29 expects an error for a non-boolean value. Runtime probe printed `0:accepted`, `:accepted`, and `null:accepted` for invalid values.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [0, '', null]) { try { pLimit({concurrency:1, rejectOnClear:value}); console.log(String(value)+':accepted'); } catch (error) { console.log(String(value)+':threw:'+error.name); } }"  # expected TypeError for all three, actual accepted

findings.title: validateConcurrency no longer accepts Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY
findings.cause: The validation predicate now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency)` and removed the explicit `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` acceptance branch.
findings.impact: Callers using `Infinity` as an unlimited-concurrency mode now get a TypeError even though this was accepted by the package baseline and still fits the public “number from 1 and up” error/option wording.
findings.evidence: git show HEAD:index.js:123-125 shows the baseline accepted `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`. Current index.js:127-130 rejects Infinity. Runtime probe printed `threw TypeError Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { const limit=pLimit(Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY); console.log('accepted', limit.concurrency); } catch (error) { console.log('threw', error.name, error.message); }"  # expected accepted Infinity, actual TypeError

commands_run: node --input-type=module runtime probes for clearQueue default, rejectOnClear validation, limitFunction args, Infinity, and map indexes
agent_testimony: Direct Mode followed: no m1nd tools or helper scripts used, no operator-only artifacts read, and the audited repo was not patched. The checkout began with index.js already modified; this audit treated that as the target state. npm test could not run fully because dev dependency binaries such as xo were unavailable, so targeted Node runtime probes were used instead.
notes: Found five source-backed behavioral/contract regressions, all in index.js. Extra confidence comes from runtime probes plus README/type/baseline evidence. Te ~= 7m30s.
